content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# Claude Code Stack/Config Audit (2026-09-22)

A full Claude Code stack and configuration audit — install, version, settings, plugins, MCP servers, skills, hooks, and permissions — was run on 2026-09-22 across 50 recent sessions plus a 30-day pass over 303 sessions. The install was healthy: a single native copy at `~/.local/bin/claude`, version 2.1.280 (current), all settings files parsing, auto mode already default, no agent files, and CLAUDE.md files totalling ~1.9k estimated tokens with no duplicates or conflicts. The user interrupted before any proposed change was applied, so the audit's output is a reviewed change list rather than a completed remediation.

## Key Points

- **Five plugins proposed for disabling** in `~/.claude/settings.json` under `enabledPlugins` — `desktop-commander@synced`, `firecrawl@synced`, `browser-use@synced`, `exa@synced`, `cowork-plugin-management@synced` — all with zero uses since install, for ~1.9k estimated tokens saved per session. Proposed, not applied.
- **A `: "` sequence inside a YAML `description:` line breaks the entire SKILL.md frontmatter**, so Claude Code silently ignores the whole header. Hit on `~/.agents/skills/persistent-localhost/SKILL.md`; fix is `description: >-` with the text on following lines. Because the skill is vendored, a vendor update can reintroduce the break.
- **The dcg hook is dead on Windows — 913 failures.** Windows settings point at the Mac path `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg`, so the dcg guard checks nothing on that machine.
- **The skill-router hook runs on every user message:** ~1.6 s typical, 68 s worst case, with 2 recorded timeouts — flagged for investigation.
- **38 blocked permission actions were reviewed and none were plain read-only commands**, so no allow rules were proposed — a negative result that is itself the finding.
- **Judgment calls, not blanket removal:** keep the `Claude Docs` connector (too new to judge), keep `persistent-localhost` but fix it rather than remove it, and flag the HyperFrames by HeyGen connector for removal (~400 tokens loaded every session, and it blocks its own main tools in Claude Code) — which the user must do manually via `/mcp`, per-project.
- **`/context` gives exact live numbers; the audit's figures were estimates** — a stated limitation of the audit method rather than a measurement.

## Details

The Windows dcg finding is the audit's most consequential result and generalizes beyond this environment. A safety guard whose hook path points at a nonexistent executable does not announce that it is absent; it fails 913 times and the guarded machine proceeds unguarded. The path in question is a Mac path (`/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/dcg`) sitting in Windows settings — the same Mac-configuration-flows-back-onto-Windows direction documented in [[concepts/windows-backup-recovery-inventory]], where the Windows backup manifest turned out to be the Mac's. The session connected it to an existing "config encoding damage from Windows" memory note, placing it in the same family as the sync-mangling described in [[concepts/dev-sync-encoding-mangling-phantom-conflicts]]. The structural point is that a guard which fails open is worse than no guard, because the operator's mental model still includes protection: this is [[connections/preconditions-that-check-the-wrong-thing]] applied to a cross-platform path rather than to a swallowed stderr.

The YAML frontmatter break is a smaller but sharply-shaped gotcha. A `: "` sequence inside an unquoted `description:` value makes the line ambiguous to the YAML parser, and the failure is not scoped to that key — the *entire* header is discarded, so the skill silently vanishes from the routing surface rather than appearing with a mangled description. The remedy (`description: >-` with the text on following lines) is the standard block-scalar escape hatch. Two second-order observations matter: this is a silent drop, joining the over-650-character descriptions in [[concepts/skill-description-budget-ceiling]] as a second mechanism by which a working skill becomes invisible to routing; and because `persistent-localhost` is vendored — hand-installed per [[concepts/vendored-skill-hand-install-pattern]] — an upstream update can reintroduce the break, so the fix is not permanent.

The audit's restraint is as informative as its findings. The five-plugin disable was left as a proposal rather than applied; the HyperFrames removal was routed to the user because it is a per-project `/mcp` action; the `Claude Docs` connector was explicitly kept on "too new to judge" grounds rather than swept up with the unused ones; and `persistent-localhost` was marked fix-don't-remove. The 38 blocked permission actions producing zero allow-rule proposals is the clearest instance — reviewing them and concluding that none qualified is a result worth recording, since an unexamined block list invites a reflexive broad allowlist. The slow skill-router hook, at ~1.6 s per user message with a 68 s worst case and two timeouts, is the one item with an unquantified cost: it is a per-message tax on every session, and the two timeouts indicate the tail is not merely slow but occasionally failing.

# Stale Hook-Failure Signals and the Archive-Hides-Open-Items Hazard

A 2026-10-03 Mac session set out to fix three session-start hook errors and found that two of them were already resolved. The `perch-pull` failure of 10/01 11:55 AM had been followed by a successful run the next afternoon at 4:35 PM (13,826 rows, newest test date 10/02, Google Drive copy to `athlete-snapshots/perch` succeeded), and the `manifest-unmanaged:42Analytics` backup error had been fixed independently by another session at 4:49 PM. The session's durable finding is a pair of rules: check the newest run's timestamp before rerunning a failed job, and treat archiving `.errors.log` as an act that silently removes still-open items from the session-start surface.

## Key Points

- **A session-start error banner is a record of a past failure, not a statement about current state.** The failing job may have succeeded on a later schedule; the newest run timestamp, not the error line, answers whether a rerun is needed.
- **Self-healing is a real disposition.** `perch-pull` recovered on its own next scheduled run, so the correct action was none at all — reruns of a job that already succeeded cost time and can duplicate work.
- **Archiving the error log suppresses unfixed items.** Another job moved `.errors.log` to `.errors.log.archived-2026-10-02` at 4:48 PM, carrying away three genuinely open items — `aios-audit` due, `memsearch-sync` index failure on the Windows laptop, and `daily-backup` / `repo-behind-blocked:global-memory` — which then stopped surfacing at session start despite being unresolved.
- **The archive therefore needs an explicit review hook.** The three suppressed items were carried forward into the next closeout by hand, because nothing else would raise them again.
- **Concurrent sessions and jobs race on this shared state.** One job archived the log before an approved edit landed, and a separate session fixed the manifest entry; both changed the world between the diagnosis and the intended action.

## Details

The staleness problem is structural rather than accidental. The session-start hook reports what the error log contains, and the error log is append-only escalation history — it records that a job failed at a moment in time and has no mechanism for retracting that line when a later run succeeds. So every banner read at session start is a claim about the past presented in the present tense, and acting on it without consulting the job's own most recent run is how a resolved failure turns into unnecessary remediation. The cheap check is always the same shape: find the newest run of the named job and read its outcome. Here that check converted a planned rerun into a no-op and produced positive evidence of health (row count, newest data date, successful Drive copy) rather than mere absence of a new error.

The archiving hazard runs in the opposite direction and is the more expensive of the two. Clearing or archiving the log is the right move once its contents are confirmed stale, which is exactly what happened earlier the same day for the resolved Docker/Milvus failure. But a blanket archive performed by an automated job cannot make that confirmation, so it removes resolved and unresolved entries alike, and the unresolved ones lose their only recurring channel to the operator. The three items lifted out on 10/02 at 4:48 PM are precisely the ones that needed to keep surfacing: an audit that was due, a cross-machine indexing failure, and a backup blocked by a repo being behind. Once archived, their continued existence depends entirely on someone having written them into a closeout note — which in this case someone did, with named verification commands (`grep MANIFEST ~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log | tail -1` for the manifest fix, and a confirmation that the `repo-behind-blocked` condition cleared on the next 21:00 run). The general rule that emerges is that the archive step must be paired either with a confirmation that every entry is stale, or with an explicit carry-forward of the entries that are not.

# Claude Code Dev Mods: Prompt-Area UI Bands

On 2026-10-02, five Claude Code "dev mods" — plugin-style UI bands rendered above the prompt — were written, validated, and pushed (commit `7313dcd`) to streamline end-of-session and repo-hygiene workflow on the Windows laptop. All code was complete; **none of it ran**. Mod loading appeared to be gated behind a feature rollout: `claude -p --plugin-dir` and `claude plugin test` were both refused with "rollout switch served off," and in-session hot reloading was declined, so the mods remained unexercised and their tests had never executed. That same evening a Mac session discovered the files had synced over via the `~/.claude` repo but sat dormant because `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` had never been set there, and enabled them by appending an `export` line to `~/.zshrc`. On 2026-10-03 the loading question was answered from the opposite direction — the mod set had grown to eight and Windows was in fact loading six of them, with two documented-as-loaded mods silently absent from the hand-maintained load list.

## Key Points

- **Five mods plus a next-steps panel:** `repo-band` (#1), `next-steps` (which absorbed the planned #2 resume buttons because both occupy the row above the prompt), `job-watch` (#3), `merge-cleanup` (#4), and `where` (#5). They live in `~/.claude/mods/` — not a session-scoped folder — so they persist and sync, with `mods/` added to the `.gitignore` allowlist in `~/.claude`.
- **Loading is controlled by the `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` env var, which is per-machine by design.** The var was only ever set on Windows, so the repo-synced mods arrived dormant on the Mac; enabling them there required a colon-separated `export` line in `~/.zshrc` (prior file backed up). Removing one entry disables one mod; deleting the var disables all. `~/.zshrc` is not covered by the `~/.claude` repo sync, so every future machine needs the same one-line step.
- **Mods render to the user's screen only; their output does not enter the agent's context.** Bands, buttons, status-line entries, and toasts are visible to the human and invisible to Claude — a boundary worth stating because it determines what a mod can and cannot be used for.
- **The hand-maintained load list concealed a partial load.** By 2026-10-03 the inventory was eight mods, and generating the list from the folder revealed that `twin-copy-guard` and `config-encoding-guard` were documented as loaded in the README but had never been added to the variable — Windows was loading 6 of 8 (see [[concepts/mods-folder-driven-load-sync]]).
- **Suggestion buttons populate the prompt box rather than submitting.** Asked whether next-steps buttons should send immediately as in the demo video, the choice was explicitly "give me the chance to edit."
- **"All the code is written and pushed" was rejected as "complete."** Since nothing had run, the honest status is code-complete-but-unverified, and the untested surface was enumerated: the Closeout and Closeout+exit buttons, the next-steps buttons, a real `merge-cleanup` branch deletion, and how `job-watch`'s status entry coexists with `statusline-command.py`.
- **Conservative-by-construction behavior:** `repo-band` uses read-only `git status` and never fetches (so it structurally cannot detect "behind remote"), scanning ~150 repos eight at a time, throttled to once per 20 s plus a 5-minute timer; `merge-cleanup` deletes only branches confirmed merged and worktrees with no uncommitted changes, and no-ops when `gh pr merge --repo` names a repo it cannot locate locally.

## Details

The design decisions share a common shape: each mod is built so that its failure mode is doing nothing rather than doing something wrong. `repo-band` forgoes fetching, which costs it the ability to report "behind remote" but guarantees it never mutates or stalls on network state across 150 repositories; the 8-at-a-time concurrency with a 20-second throttle and a 5-minute timer bounds its cost on a laptop. `merge-cleanup` encodes the existing post-merge-cleanup rule and refuses to act on anything it cannot positively confirm — unmerged branches, worktrees with uncommitted changes, or a repo named in a `gh pr merge --repo` invocation that has no local counterpart. The prompt-population choice for next-steps buttons is the same instinct at the interaction layer: a button that fills the box preserves a human edit point, whereas one that submits removes it. `job-watch` deliberately reuses `claude-stack-doctor`'s existing sources — Windows scheduled tasks under `\Eric\` and Mac launchd `com.keystone.*` — rather than defining a second inventory of jobs to drift out of sync, and that reuse paid off on the Mac: because it reads jobs via `launchctl`, no Mac-specific work was needed even though the two platforms store scheduled jobs differently. All five mods passed `claude plugin validate` on the Mac.

The per-machine nature of `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` is the most reusable operational fact. Code and configuration that live in the `~/.claude` repo propagate automatically; the shell environment that *activates* them does not, so a repo-synced feature can arrive on a new machine fully present and entirely inert. This is the same class of install-time/host-local state that recurs throughout this stack — a host fact captured per machine rather than carried by git — and it means the correct mental model for "did the mods sync?" has two independent answers: the files, yes; the activation, no. The already-open-terminal caveat compounds it, since a process's environment is fixed at launch and a fresh terminal window is required before the new var is visible.

Several implementation facts were learned that are independent of these particular mods. Bash heredocs collapse double backslashes to single, which mangles regexes in generated files — the Edit tool is the correct instrument for any content containing escapes. The plugin validator requires helper functions taking `$` to be declared at the top level of the file, forcing `refreshSoon` to be hoisted. A `grep` that finds no matches exits 1, which is not a type-check failure and should not be read as one. Background task notifications arrive at `prompt.submit` with `origin.kind = 'task-notification'`, which is both the mechanism `job-watch` uses to surface them and the reason `next-steps` must filter them out. Separately, the `dcg` `PreToolUse` hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` carried a hard-coded Mac path; it was removed on 2026-10-02, leaving one cross-platform entry that no-ops on Windows — and found restored again by the next day's closeout snapshot, making it a recurrence rather than a one-time defect.

The honest-status discipline is the 2026-10-02 session's most durable output, and the following day supplied its vindication from an unexpected angle. The direct question "Are all the mods complete?" had an easy affirmative available — everything was written, validated, and pushed — and was answered no, because validation is not execution. When loading was finally examined on 2026-10-03, the real state was neither "blocked by a rollout switch" nor "all eight running" but a silent partial load that only became visible once the list was derived from the folder rather than asserted. The README's own note about the rollout switch was likewise refined: it had only ever been observed blocking headless runs, not normal interactive sessions. The resulting handoff on both machines is a verification plan rather than a completion claim — restart Claude Code in a fresh terminal so the regenerated or newly added `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` is picked up, then report what appears above the prompt or paste any `<mod>: hooks module not loaded` line.

# Public Repo Privacy Audit: Names Mislead, Contents Decide

On 2026-09-09, 21 public GitHub repositories were audited for exposed athlete data ahead of a bulk visibility change. Reading inside every repository — rather than triaging by name or by an automated flag — inverted most of the initial assessment: repositories that *mentioned* athletes in code carried no athlete data files, while the genuine exposure sat in two repositories whose names gave no signal. Eighteen were flipped private under the user's rule, "flip everything private that isn't going to make a website go dark."

## Key Points

- **Only two repositories held real exposure:** `B_Ellis` and `cmj-norms-app`, containing named athletes with force-plate data (Devin Turner, Kamauryn Morgan) plus real rosters. `Practice_PlayCounts` looked risky and was cleared — its roster is fabricated sample data.
- **Name-based sensitivity screening produced pure false positives.** `JumpReporting`, `VALD_analytics`, and `PT_Dash` all reference athletes in code while containing no athlete data files.
- **GitHub Pages is not the only thing a public repo can be serving.** The first liveness check cleared `JumpReporting` as "no Pages site, safe to flip"; it actually deploys to Vercel, caught only on a second pass that looked for external deploy targets.
- **The liveness check itself had a bug:** 404 response bodies were being counted as live sites, requiring a re-run with proper status-code handling before any result could be trusted.
- **Three repos stayed public because each backs a live site:** `SportScienceResearchRepo` (GitHub Pages), `Travel_Map` (GitHub Pages), `JumpReporting` (Vercel).
- **Private repos can still break downstream publishing.** `printing-press-library` publishes to npm and `GameONPaper` pushes Docker containers; the mitigating fact is that flipping visibility back is instant and lossless if a build fails.

## Details

The audit is a clean demonstration that a repository's name is a description of its *subject*, not of its *contents*, and the two diverge in both directions. A tool for analyzing jump data will mention athletes throughout its source without ever committing a row of athlete data, because the data lives in a gitignored directory or an external database — precisely the local-first convention used across the Baylor sports-tech pipelines. Conversely, a repository named after a person or a normative dataset may exist specifically to hold the data. Any screen that operates on names, or on a keyword match against source text, will therefore rank these backwards. The only reliable filter was reading inside all 21, which is the same conclusion reached when the Microsoft-versus-Google Forms mismatch was exposed only by opening the raw export rather than the cleaned CSV.

The liveness check produced two distinct failure modes worth separating. The 404-counted-as-live bug is an instrumentation defect: an HTTP fetch that inspects the response body without first checking the status code will treat GitHub's styled 404 page as content, and the resulting false positives would have kept repositories public for no reason. That is the safe direction to fail, which is exactly why it is easy to miss. The `JumpReporting` miss is the dangerous direction and a scope error rather than a bug: the check asked "does this repo have a GitHub Pages site?" when the operational question was "does anything depend on this repo being public?" Vercel, Netlify, npm, and container registries all answer yes to the second question and no to the first, and each one was a potential outage. The pattern is the recurring one in this knowledge base — a status field or check answering a narrower predicate than the question being asked — and the remedy was a second pass explicitly enumerating external deploy targets.

Two items were deliberately left unresolved rather than decided under the same sweep. `SportScienceResearchRepo` publishes roughly 4,700 research PDFs publicly, which raises a copyright question rather than a privacy one; because the two concerns have different owners and different remedies, it was correctly excluded from the privacy pass and left as the user's call. And `erash11/DexaProject` remains on GitHub with a patient CSV and requires deletion, blocked on `gh auth refresh -h github.com -s delete_repo` before `gh repo delete` will run — a scope the token was not originally granted.

# Single-Quoted $HOME in a Hook Command Blocks Expansion

On 2026-09-16 a recurring "non-blocking status" error at every Claude Code session start was traced to a single character class: line 310 of `~/.claude/settings.json` wrapped a hook command in single quotes, so `$HOME` was passed to bash literally rather than expanded. Bash then looked for a directory named `$HOME`, exited 127, and Claude Code surfaced the non-zero exit as a startup error. Changing the quotes to double quotes (`bash "$HOME/.claude/hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh" session`) fixed it; the hook was verified by running it manually and observing exit 0, and the change was committed as `78b6532` in the `~/.claude` repo.

## Key Points

- **Single quotes in a JSON hook command string suppress shell expansion.** `'$HOME/...'` reaches bash as a literal path; only double quotes let the variable resolve while still tolerating spaces in the expanded path.
- **Claude Code surfaces any hook exit code other than 0 or 2 as a "non-blocking status" error**, so a path typo and a genuine script failure present identically at session start.
- **Only one of the four startup hook lines carried the bug**; the other three exited 0. The presence of several hook entries means a startup error does not identify which one failed — each must be run manually to isolate it.
- **The three "HOOK FAILURES" lines shown at startup are a different signal entirely** — they are logged results from earlier *scheduled* jobs (gps-pull network, memsearch onnx, backup repos), not SessionStart hook failures. Conflating the two sends the diagnosis to the wrong subsystem.
- **`.errors.log` was empty after the fix**, which is the confirming check rather than the absence of a visible error message.

## Details

The quoting defect belongs to the family of environment assumptions that only bite inside a hook. The hook command string lives in JSON, which has its own escaping rules, and is then handed to a shell, which has different ones; the author's mental model of "quote the path so spaces are safe" is correct in intent and wrong in execution, because single quotes achieve the space-safety and simultaneously destroy the variable. The failure is silent in the sense that matters: nothing about the settings file looks wrong, the script exists and is executable, and the only externally visible symptom is a generic status error at a moment when the user is trying to start work on something else. This sits alongside the `uv`-on-PATH problem in [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] and the PowerShell-syntax hooks in [[concepts/gsd-hook-bash-rewrite]] as instances of the hook execution environment differing from the interactive shell the command was mentally tested in — the general form catalogued in [[connections/hook-execution-environment-path-assumptions]].

The second finding is arguably more durable than the fix. Two distinct classes of message appear at session start — SessionStart hook exit statuses, and a summary of logged failures from earlier scheduled jobs — and they are visually adjacent enough to be read as one report. Reading the three "HOOK FAILURES" lines as SessionStart failures would have sent the investigation into `settings.json`'s hook array looking for four bugs when there was one, and would have left three real but unrelated scheduled-job failures (a network-dependent GPS pull, a memsearch ONNX problem, a backup repo issue) unaddressed in their own right. The discipline is to establish which subsystem produced a message before acting on it, the same scope-checking reflex recorded in [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]], where a `launchctl` exit code described a narrower predicate than the operational question being asked of it.

The verification and commit hygiene are worth noting. The fix was confirmed by invoking the hook script directly and checking for exit 0 rather than by restarting and observing the absence of an error, which is a weaker signal because a startup error can be absent for many reasons. The commit deliberately included only `settings.json` and excluded modified session transcript files that happened to be dirty in the same repo — the same explicit-path staging discipline applied in [[concepts/skills-repo-git-hygiene]]. Because the `~/.claude` repo is shared across machines, the fix's propagation required an action on the other machine: the recorded follow-up was to run `/dev-sync` on the Windows laptop and then start a fresh session to confirm the error was gone there, an instance of the working-machine-authors-the-fix pattern in [[concepts/fix-from-the-working-machine-handoff]].

# Baylor Athletics Technology Inventory Analysis

On 2026-08-30, the Baylor Athletics Technology Inventory project (`~/DEV/Tech_Inventory_Analysis`) was finalized for distribution: a web report was published, a PDF rendered, a `.docx` added, and all deliverables copied to OneDrive under `00_Primary_Storage_Drive/05_SYSTEMS/SoftwareTechDocs/TechInventory_2026-08/`. The session's most consequential outcome was not a deliverable but a correction — searching meeting transcripts revealed the survey was still open, forcing all four documents to be reframed as an **interim** read rather than a closed finding. A 2026-09-07 verification pass confirmed the data had not moved and surfaced a platform-documentation mismatch that would have produced a false "no new responses" answer.

## Key Points

- **The survey is not closed.** 29 August was Applied Performance's *internal* deadline; the 24 August all-staff meeting set a **department-wide soft deadline of 29 September**. Five non-responding units (27 of 33 in) are outstanding, not delinquent — the original wording read as blame.
- **As of 2026-09-07 nothing had changed:** 37 response rows, still 27 of 33 units, newest source still `raw/Quick_Inventory_export_2026-08-29.xlsx`, byte-identical by md5 to the OneDrive copy, no newer export anywhere in the home folder. The five outstanding units are Golf (M), Tennis (M), Tennis (W), Volleyball, and Business Office; "Other" is a catch-all box, not a real department.
- **The live survey runs on Microsoft Forms, but project docs point at Google Forms** from the 08-13 proposal era — a trap that would make a `gws` query return a truthful-but-false empty result. See [[concepts/microsoft-forms-vs-google-forms-inventory-mismatch]].
- **Deliverable format was determined from transcripts, not guessed.** Kenny's own words from the 13 August meeting — "the more simple and concise, almost like **one page checklist**" and "I do think we need to figure out all the systems that we're using" — plus Jon Allen's "nobody knows everything that exists" (80–90% known) support building a one-page executive summary matching the existing `Software_and_Tech_Management_EXEC_SUMMARY_ER_2026-08-14.docx` pattern, with the 10-page report retained as the working document.
- **PII discipline on publication:** `raw/*.xlsx` contains respondent names and email addresses and was neither published nor copied; the PDF, HTML, and docx were scanned to confirm no PII before distribution. `README.md` (script run instructions) was deliberately withheld, available on request.
- **Copy, not move, to OneDrive.** Deliverables were placed next to the existing Software and Technology Management framework docs using the established `_ER_<date>` filename convention; local originals were left untouched.
- **Docx tables are generated from the clean CSVs** (`uv run --with python-docx python3 scripts/build_docx.py`) so prose and data cannot drift — a guard that was needed, since hand-written prose in the same docx said "roughly thirteen vendors" while listing twelve (Switch missing).
- **Data resolutions:** "Marketing and Fan Experience" merged into Marketing (34 → 33 units, Marketing no longer a gap); Red Card identified as the athlete meal-money stipend, holding athlete identity/spending data (athlete-data count 59 → 60). Two of 324 product names — **SCRL app** and **JABA** — remain unidentified.

## Details

The framing error is the session's central lesson and generalizes well beyond this project. The analysis had been written as though the response window had closed, which turns five missing units into an implicit accusation of non-compliance. The actual governance timeline — an internal Applied Performance deadline of 29 August nested inside a department-wide soft deadline of 29 September — was recoverable only from meeting transcripts, not from the survey artifact itself. This is the same discipline applied to the deliverable-format question: rather than infer what Kenny would want from a report, the transcripts were searched for his stated preference, which turned out to be an explicit "one page checklist." In both cases the authoritative record lived in a channel outside the working artifact, and consulting it changed the output materially. The Fireflies transcript corpus functions here as a governance source of truth, the same role it plays in [[concepts/athletics-performance-landing-page-spec]], where a spec was grounded in a specific meeting rather than assembled from assumption. A parallel language edit followed the same source: "nothing in the current process notices this" was reworked into forward-looking capability language to match Kenny's known review preferences.

The 2026-09-07 resume session shows what maintaining an interim deliverable actually costs. The question "has anything changed?" was answered by going to the raw `.xlsx` rather than the cleaned CSV, comparing the local and OneDrive copies by md5 rather than by filename, and searching the whole home folder for a newer export — three independent checks to establish a negative. That thoroughness paid for itself by exposing the Microsoft-Forms-versus-Google-Forms documentation drift, which is invisible downstream of the cleaning step and would otherwise have been discovered only after a future session trusted a stale form ID. The practical consequence is that this project's refresh loop is human-gated: the export cannot be pulled from any CLI, so the interim label persists until someone manually downloads a new file and runs `uv run --with openpyxl python3 scripts/clean_inventory.py`, confirming `clean/unmapped_review.csv` is empty.

The generation-hygiene findings echo failures catalogued elsewhere in this knowledge base. Headless Chrome stamped a `file:///Users/...` path into the PDF footer by default and a page-break rule left a half-empty page — neither of which is detectable from the output's byte size, only from inspecting the rendered PDF, the same render-layer verification rule established in [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]] and exercised on Excel conditional formatting in [[concepts/openpyxl-conditional-formatting-alpha-gotcha]]. The prose/data drift ("roughly thirteen vendors" over a list of twelve) is the specific failure that generating tables directly from CSVs is meant to prevent; that the drift survived in the hand-written surrounding prose shows the guard covers only the generated region, and hand-written summary sentences over generated data remain a live drift surface. Because every document rebuilds from the pipeline, the post-29-September plan is mechanical: re-export the survey data, re-run the pipeline, and all four documents regenerate with final numbers — which is also why the one-page executive summary can be built now (marked interim) at negligible cost.

# Concurrent Claude Sessions Working the Same Repos

The 13:10 closeout on 2026-09-19 ran while a second Claude session (started 10:14) was operating on the same repositories. The overlap produced four distinct effects: a suspected reverted edit that turned out to be a bad grep, a handoff-ownership decision, a redundant clone of a repo that was already present under a differently-spelled name, and a real `global-memory` merge conflict from the other session's push.

## Key Points

- **A failed grep is visually identical to a reverted edit.** Checking whether the concurrent session had undone the daily-backup manifest fix returned nothing; the cause was bad quoting in the grep, not a revert. Verification requires reading the file, not trusting a grep's silence.
- **Handoffs are written per session, not per machine.** The other session's handoff did not cover the backup-divergence fix, so a separate handoff was written and the other session's was left untouched.
- **Duplicate work slipped through the name gap.** `DEV/Linda Projects` (with a space) was already in the backup manifest; the concurrent session cloned it again as `Linda_Projects`, leaving two clones of one private repo.
- **Concurrent sessions cause genuine merge conflicts in `global-memory`** — pulling before committing memory should be the expected step, not an exception.
- **A detached HEAD found during the sweep was safe** because the commit was already on `origin/main` — check before treating it as damage.

## Details

Multi-session concurrency on shared repositories converts several ordinarily-reliable signals into ambiguous ones. An unexpected file state now has at least three explanations — this session's own action, the other session's action, or a measurement error — and the default assumption that "nothing changed it but me" no longer holds. The grep incident is the instructive case: the natural reading of an empty result was that the concurrent session had reverted the manifest fix, which is a plausible story that fits the evidence and is wrong. Reading the file directly settled it. This is the same step-down-to-ground-truth move recorded in [[connections/step-down-to-ground-truth-when-the-surface-lies]], with the wrinkle that concurrency supplies a *believable* wrong hypothesis, which is what makes the shortcut tempting.

The handoff decision establishes a scoping rule for a situation the closeout discipline had not previously faced. [[concepts/closeout-scope-discipline-other-sessions-work]] settled that a sweep covers its own session's surface and leaves another session's in-flight work alone; the corollary drawn here is that the same applies to the *documentation* of that work. Editing the other session's handoff to append this session's fix would attribute work across a boundary the reader cannot see, so a separate handoff was written and the existing one left as its author wrote it. The redundant `Linda_Projects` clone is the failure that this scoping cannot prevent: two sessions, each acting reasonably on its own information, produced duplicated work because the repository's canonical name contains a space and the second session normalised it. That is a close relative of the name-mismatch false alarms in [[concepts/dev-sync-false-missing-repos]], and the same space-in-path hazard that broke shell sweeps twice in this session — word splitting silently drops entries, so every path must be quoted.

The `global-memory` conflict is the least surprising and most structural finding: two sessions appending to the same memory repository will collide, and the correct posture is to pull before committing rather than to discover the collision at push time. Transcript-log conflicts of this kind already have an established resolution — union merge, keeping every line from both sides, as three independent instances confirmed in [[concepts/dev-sync-2026-09-22-manifest-and-union-merge]]. This is the intra-machine analogue of the cross-machine push collisions in [[concepts/unattended-cross-machine-push-collisions]]: the other writer is now a sibling process rather than another laptop, but the merge cost and the "check whether someone else already handled this" reflex are identical. Two further sweep-level observations round the session out: background sweeps buffer output and can hang, so a fast local pass over dirty and unpushed files is sufficient for sign-off, and dirty files remaining at closeout were live session logs rather than unsaved work.

# Flint: Mac/Windows Work Split, Stranded Branch, and the OneDrive Triage Sort

Flint is an AI thought-partner project fed by the user's vault. Across two 2026-10-02 Mac sessions it was identified as the active thread, its stranded work was merged, and its OneDrive catalog triage was advanced to a proposed keep/drop sort. The session also fixed a role boundary that had been blurring: **Flint *knows* things** (a thought partner fed by the vault), while **AgentAssist *does* things** (a department workflow routing a question ledger to TEACH / STUDY / ANSWER). A possible future link was noted — an AgentAssist ledger question could be handed to Flint for a research-backed answer — but the two remain distinct projects.

## Key Points

- **38 commits of 9/28–9/29 work sat stranded on `step1-triage` with no open PR**, so Flint's `main` read as 9/27 and every `/dev-sync` reported stale status. Merged as PR #2 (merge commit `4aa4c6b`), resolving a `docs/STATUS.md` conflict in favor of the branch and fixing two stale lines that falsely claimed the merge was already done.
- **`step1-triage` was deliberately not deleted.** The Windows laptop holds a worktree on that branch containing the only copy of the local book files; deletion is queued as a Windows-side task (switch to `main`, pull, then delete).
- **Mac sessions are review-and-decision only for Flint.** `staging/books`, `ocr`, and `audio` exist solely on the Windows laptop, so no new atomizing is possible from the Mac.
- **The OneDrive import list is far smaller than it looks:** 73 folders and 8,994 files scanned, but only **295 files actually held**, concentrated in 10 folders — everything else already covered by the rules.
- **Athlete data is excluded from Jev categorically.** `FB_FA24_GPS_SessionReport` (269 files) and `PracticePlanning` (82) were proposed for dropping on that ground alone, independent of their content value. The least-certain call is `08_ARCHIVE/PERSONAL` (69 held, 392 papers/books), which may contain training material.
- **The paired AgentAssist PR #1 was left parked** — six weeks stale and containing out-of-date facts (it claims no wellness/sRPE data exists) — to be reviewed before any future merge.

## Details

The stranded-branch finding is the session's most portable lesson, because its cost was paid repeatedly before it was noticed. Thirty-eight commits of real work lived on `step1-triage` while `main` showed a 9/27 tip, which means every sync sweep, every commit-recency ranking, and every "what was I last working on?" query read Flint as a quiet repo. The sync was not malfunctioning — it reported the state of `main` accurately — but the project's visible state had become a lie about the project's actual state. The rule extracted was temporal: open a PR the same day, or the next sync lies. This is the same class of defect as the recency-versus-work-recency trap hit on the same day, where `graphify-out` and `CommandCentre` topped the newest-commit ranking on closeout snapshots while PP_Recruiting's 23 commits were the real incoming work; a branch with no PR and a repo with only automated commits are two different ways for commit metadata to misrepresent human attention.

The deliberate non-deletion of `step1-triage` is the counterweight to the usual post-merge-cleanup rule. Branch deletion is normally safe because git retains the commits, but here the branch is checked out as a worktree on another machine, and that worktree holds files that exist nowhere else — so deleting the branch would strand or destroy the only copy of the local books. The decision records the reason rather than just the deferral, which is what lets the Windows-side cleanup proceed in the right order (switch to `main`, pull, *then* delete) rather than being re-derived under pressure. Two operational frictions compounded the work: the shell safety hook blocks compound git commands and all branch deletes, so branch deletion must be performed by the user and multi-step git work must be split into plain single commands; and `sync-to-codex.sh` is not marked executable, requiring `bash <path>`.

The OneDrive triage illustrates how much a rules layer can compress a nominally huge job. Scanning 73 folders and 8,994 files produced only 295 held files in 10 folders, because the existing rules already covered the rest — so the human decision surface was two orders of magnitude smaller than the raw inventory. Within that surface the governing constraint is categorical rather than evaluative: athlete data never goes to Jev, which disqualifies `FB_FA24_GPS_SessionReport` and `PracticePlanning` without any judgment about whether their contents would be useful. The proposed keep set is the five `XX_MIGRATION/*` folders plus `Conference_Materials` and `APPLIED_PERFORMANCE`; personal, HR, photo, and video-archive material is dropped. The one genuinely uncertain call — `08_ARCHIVE/PERSONAL`, 69 held files among 392 papers and books — was surfaced as a question rather than guessed, and the whole sort was left pending the user's accept before committing.

# Shell Safety Guard False Positives and Native-Tool Workarounds

The `dcg` shell safety guard blocks command shapes that it cannot reason about, producing false positives on benign work. The accumulated catalogue of blocked shapes now spans inline PowerShell invoked via Bash, compound Bash commands joined with `&&` or `;`, multi-repo `for` loops over `git status`, and all git branch deletions. In every case the workaround is the same in kind: decompose the command into plain single invocations, move the logic into a script file, or hand the action to the user.

## Key Points

- **Blocked shapes observed so far:** inline PowerShell run through Bash; compound Bash commands; `for` loops sweeping multiple repos with `git status`; and branch deletion, governed by the rule `core.git:branch-force-delete`.
- **Decomposition is the general workaround.** Splitting a compound command into sequential plain commands passes, as does putting the identical sweep into a script file and executing that.
- **Branch deletion cannot be decomposed around** — the rule blocks the action itself, so the user must run the delete. This recurred on 2026-10-02, when the user deleted the `foundation` branch locally and remotely after the agent was blocked.
- **A script file is a legitimate escape hatch for loops**, which means the guard constrains the *shape* of the invocation rather than the operation's risk; recognising this turns a block into a two-step reroute rather than a dead end.
- **Guard blocks are distinguishable from real failures by their immediacy and their message**, and should not be debugged as code defects; the correct first move is to reshape the invocation.

## Details

The pattern across instances is that the guard operates on syntactic surface rather than semantics. A `for` loop over `git status` across 150 repositories is read-only and harmless, yet it is blocked, while the same sweep written into a script file and invoked once is permitted — the risk is identical, so the discriminator is the shape of the command string. This has a practical upside: because the guard's criterion is syntactic, the workaround is mechanical and predictable, and an agent that recognises the block can reroute in one step rather than experimenting. It also has a cost worth naming, which is that moving logic into a script file to satisfy a guard makes the logic less visible in the transcript than an inline command would be.

Branch deletion is the one case where no reroute exists, because the rule names the operation rather than the syntax. The correct response there is the route-to-the-owning-layer move: state plainly which branch should be deleted and ask the user to run it, exactly as a user-invocation-only skill must be typed by the user and a permission-blocked directory listing must be resolved by a permission rule. The 2026-10-02 instance is instructive because the deletion was part of a normal post-merge cleanup — the guard is most likely to fire during routine hygiene, which is also when an agent is most likely to treat the block as noise and move on, leaving a merged branch undeleted. Recording the blocked action as an explicit user task is what prevents that drift, and it is the same reasoning that led `merge-cleanup`, the dev mod built to automate this hygiene, to be designed to act only on positively-confirmed merged branches.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

## Evidence

- 2026-04-22 (10:57): "Background agent produced `docs/batch_r7_fixes.json` but hallucinated wrong author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358... Used PyPDF2 text extraction to verify actual authors and corrected all three citations before committing."
- 2026-04-22 (17:21): "Photo failed to render in localhost preview — identified as a server limitation (brainstorm preview server doesn't serve image files), not an HTML error... always verify photo rendering by opening the HTML directly in Chrome via file:// URL."

# Connection: A Status Field Answers a Narrower Question Than the One Being Asked

## The Connection

`launchctl list` column 2 reports the exit code of the *last scheduled* invocation of a job. The question being asked of it is "is this backup healthy?" These are different questions, and on 2026-08-31 they diverged: the manifest was fixed at 10:31, the manual re-run exited clean, and the status field stayed red because no scheduled run had occurred since. The same divergence appears in the 2026-08-06 background-monitor findings, where a comment-count bump answered "did the count change?" while being read as "is there a new finding?" — and counted the agent's own replies toward the total.

## Key Insight

These are not cases of a signal being *wrong*. Each field reports accurately on its own narrow predicate; the failure is that the predicate is narrower than the operational question, and nothing at the display layer marks the gap. `launchctl` never claimed to know about out-of-band runs. A comment counter never claimed to distinguish authorship. The reader supplies the broader interpretation, and it holds right up until an event occurs that the field's scope excludes — a manual re-run, a self-authored reply, a duplicate delivery during a lockout.

This yields a specific diagnostic move, distinct from the general "verify at ground truth" rule: before reconciling a suspicious signal against an artifact, first ask what proposition the signal actually asserts. Doing so often dissolves the anomaly without any investigation — the 2026-08-31 red status needed no debugging once its scope was named, and the correct action became *leave it alone*, because the field will self-correct at the next scheduled tick. Forcing a manual re-run to turn it green would have been cosmetic, treating the display as the state. Where the earlier lessons say "check the artifact when the layer lies," this one says "check the layer's scope before deciding it lied at all."

## Evidence

- 2026-08-31: "`launchctl list` column 2 reflects the *last scheduled* run, not manual/out-of-band runs — a green backup log can coexist with a red launchd status. Confirm against the backup log timeline before treating the exit code as a live failure." The recommendation was explicitly to leave the stale code alone since it self-clears at the next 09:00 run.
- 2026-08-06: background monitor comment-count bumps counted the agent's own replies as new findings — the counter answered "count changed" and was read as "new external finding."
- 2026-08-06: monitor events were silently dropped during a session-limit lockout (~15 duplicates, no dedup, backoff, or alert) — delivery status reported on transmission, not on receipt.
- 2026-07-18: the SpeedProfiling background task's "exit code 1" reported on the process-management wrapper, not on whether the R script's work completed — the log showed a clean end-to-end run.

# PP_Recruiting Workbook 012: Benchmark-Tagged Unified Grading

Workbook 012 of the PP_Recruiting project is workbook 010 plus a BENCHMARK tag and a new percentile-profile tab, completed and merged to `main` on 2026-09-26 (PR #2, merge commit `8a3de3a`). It changed no thresholds and no formulas; its purpose is to let per-position grading distributions be read off proven 2025 players. The workbook was staged for staff in `Send\`, and the session recorded three gotchas that must accompany it.

## Key Points

- **Benchmark files contained no new data.** All 710 top-2025 players were already present in the 2025 exports: 578 had zero eligibility remaining (the reason workbook 010 excluded them) and the remaining 132 were already 010 rows.
- **What 012 adds:** a BENCHMARK tag (PORTAL INPUT column BT, REVIEW BOARD column AL) and a final BENCHMARK PROFILES tab giving per-position 25th/median/75th percentiles plus share ≥75, computed live off REVIEW BOARD. Top End Speed is excluded pending mph confirmation. No thresholds or formulas were altered.
- **The data grades proven players low.** Of the 710 proven 2025 players, only 16% project AL or better, about half QS or better, and 78% still flag REVIEW — consistent with an earlier validation run. Mendoza is the exemplar: traits project FRP while a Player Impact of 98 trips REVIEW.
- **012's REVIEW count is inflated by ineligible players.** The displayed 2,352 REVIEW count drops to 010's 1,899 (1,708 with 150+ snaps) once the new Benchmark column is filtered to blank. The 011 screening-matrix numbers still refer to 010, and staff must be told this before opening 012.
- **012 is not loader-safe.** New data keeps loading onto 010, never 012 — the benchmark workbook is a read/analysis artifact, not the ingestion target.
- **Structural grading ceiling at OT/OG/C:** those positions carry only two traits each, so they can only land AA, QS, LIM, or NGE. This is a design consequence of the trait count, not a data defect.

## Details

The benchmark exercise began as an attempt to add proven-player reference data and ended by confirming that no new data existed to add — the value was entirely in tagging and summarizing rows already present. That result matters for interpretation: because the 578 zero-eligibility players were deliberately excluded from 010, tagging them back in for benchmark purposes reintroduces rows that the operational grading view intentionally omits. Hence the inflated REVIEW count and the blank-Benchmark filter that restores the operational numbers. The discipline adopted was to change nothing in the grading logic — no thresholds, no formulas — so that any difference between 010 and 012 is attributable solely to population, not to method. That is what makes the percentile profiles readable as a property of the players rather than of a revised rubric.

The substantive finding is that the grading system rates proven, productive 2025 players low: only 16% project AL or better and 78% still flag REVIEW. Mendoza makes the tension concrete — trait projections land at FRP while a Player Impact score of 98 nonetheless trips REVIEW, meaning the flag is firing on players whose production is close to the ceiling. Read together with the OT/OG/C two-trait ceiling, the pattern suggests the flagging thresholds and the trait coverage per position both need review before the REVIEW flag is treated as a screening signal. Two operational hazards were handled by file hygiene rather than documentation alone: workbook 012 was copied into `Send\` and the stale "Prototype - 003" workbook was moved to `_to_delete\`, so staff cannot open the wrong file. A STATUS correction (`a0cb038`) was pushed immediately after the merge because `main` still claimed 010 as latest, which would have hidden 010–012 from the Mac and from any fresh agent — the same cross-machine staleness problem that the machine-split closeout guards against.

Repository cleanup closed the branch: `worktree-fireflies-review-board-0915` was deleted locally and on GitHub, leaving a single-branch, clean repo. Git released the worktree cleanly, but Windows blocked deletion of the folder itself because Drive sync holds locks on `Desktop\DEV`; Eric cleared it manually, and this is expected on every worktree teardown on this laptop.
