# Rounded Counts and Ratios in Always-Loaded Context Documents

On 2026-09-07 a config-hygiene pass corrected several drifted inventory counts in `~/DEV/CLAUDE.md` — 155 skills, 230 compiled articles, 849 notes, 38,832 of 56,707 files — and then changed the convention that had allowed them to drift. Exact figures were replaced with `~`-prefixed rounded values plus an inline note explaining why, and the Football-files row was rewritten from a raw pair of numbers into a ratio ("about two thirds of DEV") on the grounds that the proportion remains true as files accumulate while the absolute counts do not.

## Key Points

- **Four counts had drifted and two had not.** Skills, compiled articles, vault notes, and the file counts were corrected; the custom-CLI count (8) and the per-project `CLAUDE.md` count (18) were already accurate — slow-moving inventories drift more slowly.
- **Exact numbers in a long-lived context document go stale within weeks,** so the corrected values were deliberately rounded with `~` rather than restated precisely.
- **The rounding was documented in the file itself,** so a future reader (human or agent) does not "helpfully" restore precision and reintroduce the drift.
- **A ratio was substituted where one was available:** the Football-files row became "about two thirds of DEV," a statement that stays true as the denominator grows, unlike `38,832 of 56,707`.
- **Precision is a liability, not a virtue, when nothing recomputes it.** The value of an exact count is realized only at the moment of measurement; afterward it decays into a confident false claim.

## Details

The distinction the session drew is between numbers that are regenerated and numbers that are transcribed. A table built by a script from a data source can be exact because it is rebuilt whenever the source changes; a count typed into a context file is a snapshot with no refresh mechanism, and it begins decaying immediately. Writing `38,832 of 56,707` in such a file commits the document to a claim it cannot maintain, and — worse — the specificity signals to a reader that the figure was recently verified. Rounding to `~39,000` or restating as a proportion sacrifices nothing operationally useful, because no decision in this workspace depends on the fourth significant figure, while removing the false precision signal. This is the same asymmetry noted in [[concepts/interim-framing-for-open-data-collection]], where a figure's *status* mattered more than its accuracy, and the complement of [[concepts/generated-tables-versus-handwritten-prose-drift]], where authored prose drifted away from a generated table that had kept itself current.

The ratio substitution is the sharper move and deserves stating as a general preference: where a quantity can be expressed as a proportion of something that grows alongside it, the proportion is the more durable representation. "About two thirds of DEV is Football files" survives the addition of thousands of files on both sides of the fraction; "38,832 of 56,707" is falsified by the next sync. The transformation is not always available — a skill count has no natural denominator — but when it is, it converts a fact with a short half-life into one with a long one. Selecting the representation with the longest useful life is the design question, not merely getting today's number right.

The observation that two of six counts had not drifted is a useful secondary signal. The custom-CLI count and per-project `CLAUDE.md` count were still correct because those inventories change on a timescale of months, whereas skills, compiled knowledge articles, and vault notes all accumulate continuously. This suggests a triage rule for periodic hygiene passes: check the fast-moving inventories every time and the slow-moving ones rarely, rather than re-verifying every number at equal cost. The same session's `/claude-stack-doctor` run confirmed the rest of the stack healthy — `MEMORY.md` at 85% of cap (2,133/2,500 bytes, down from the over-cap condition three days earlier), a clean errors log, a backup with 31 targets, a verified cloud receipt, and all four repos synced.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

## claude.ai Wispr Flow
Use this server when the user asks about meetings, notes, transcripts, or calendar information stored in Wispr Flow. For questions that may span multiple connected sources, use the relevant sources needed to answer the request. Read https://notes.wisprflow.ai/shared/ links with resolve_share_link rather than fetching the page. All timestamps returned by these tools are UTC (ISO 8601, ending in 'Z'). Before showing any time to the user, convert it to their local time zone — never present the raw UTC value.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

# Output Style Resolution: Project-Local Settings Win

The Claude Code harness output style is controlled by an `outputStyle` key that can be set in more than one settings file, and the project-local file takes precedence. On 2026-10-08 the resolution order was spelled out after a question about how to change it: `~/.claude/settings.json` holds the global value and `~/DEV/.claude/settings.local.json` holds a project-local override, so editing only the global file leaves the local style (`ELI5`) active inside `~/DEV` — which is where most work happens.

## Key Points

- **Two change routes:** `/config` → Output style menu, or edit the `outputStyle` key directly in a settings file.
- **The project-local file wins.** A global edit has no visible effect inside a directory whose `settings.local.json` sets its own `outputStyle`, so the apparent "edit didn't work" symptom is actually correct precedence.
- **Changes take effect next session;** `/clear` or a restart applies them immediately rather than waiting.
- **Custom styles live in `~/.claude/output-styles/`**, and at the time of the check only `ELI5.md` existed there.

## Details

The failure mode this guards against is a silent no-op: the global file is the obvious place to look, the edit succeeds, and nothing changes because a narrower-scoped file is answering the same question. That shape recurs throughout this configuration stack — a per-machine environment variable that git cannot carry, a stale memory pointer that resolves cleanly to the wrong file — and the common remedy is to enumerate every file that can supply the value before editing any one of them. Here the enumeration is small (two settings files plus the custom-style directory), which makes the rule cheap to apply and cheap to forget.

The deferred-effect behaviour is worth separating from the precedence question. Because an output-style change does not apply to the running session, the immediate observation after an edit is *always* "nothing changed" regardless of whether the edit was correct. Without knowing that `/clear` or a restart is the applying action, a correct global edit and a precedence-shadowed one produce identical evidence, and the natural next move — editing more files — makes the configuration worse. Checking the project-local file first and then forcing the reload separates the two causes.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/claude-code-dev-mods-ui-bands]] — Another per-machine activation layer in the same settings surface, where synced artifacts arrive inert.
- [[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]] — The same `settings.json` family, with a different multi-writer hazard.
- [[concepts/a-stale-pointer-resolves-cleanly-to-the-wrong-answer]] — The general shape: a lookup that succeeds while returning a value other than the one intended.
- [[concepts/claude-code-permission-modes]] — Another case where the harness's configured mode, not the apparent command, explains an unexpected result.
- [[concepts/global-prompt-stack-audit]] — The broader audit of this configuration surface.

- [[daily/2026-10-08.md]] — Output-style session (15:34): `/config` and direct-edit routes, `outputStyle` present in both `~/.claude/settings.json` and `~/DEV/.claude/settings.local.json` with the local file winning inside `~/DEV`, next-session effect with `/clear`-or-restart for immediate application, and `~/.claude/output-styles/` holding only `ELI5.md`.

# Branch Drift Hides Working Code From main

A cleanup of `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler` deleted nine merged branches and, in the process, exposed a more serious condition: **`main` was not what was running.** The backfill feature used to recover a dead flush existed only on a branch, so for 17 days a working capability was absent from the mainline and invisible to anything that read `main`. The same sweep found five other repositories parked on feature branches in the same state, and found that the closeout routine had a blind spot that let the condition persist unreported.

## Key Points

- **Nine merged branches were deleted after each was verified at 0 commits not in `main`** — including `session-start-progressive-disclosure`, merged that same day. Nothing was lost. The accompanying rule: if a delete is ever refused, stop and report, never force.
- **A branch holding working code keeps `main` lying about the project's capability.** The flush-recovery backfill was real, tested, and unreachable from `main` for 17 days.
- **The closeout sweep never checked `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler`.** It walked `~/DEV` plus three config repos, which is why past closeouts signed off "clear" over an unmerged branch. Fixed in this session; the sweep now covers nested `~/.claude` repos (149 repos swept).
- **Five repositories remain parked on feature branches** — `AgentAssist`, `PT_Dash`, `Football/SpeedProfiling`, `CFB_Analytics_Lab`, `ZoteroInjestion` — all pushed and clean, but carrying the same `main`-drift that was just fixed in the compiler.
- **A branch named `origin` in an earlier ref listing was a listing artifact, not a real branch** — one more case of a tool's output needing interpretation before action.

## Details

The deletion half of this work was routine and the finding half was not. Verifying each branch at zero commits not in `main` before deleting is the correct order of operations, and it is what made the sweep safe; the standing rule that a refused delete must be reported rather than forced keeps the safety property intact under surprise. But the question that produced the real result was not about branches at all — a question about one log line (`Indexed 0 chunks`) that turned out to be correct behaviour nonetheless exposed five distinct problems when pulled on, including the branch drift itself, a leftover backup folder containing raw session text that needed gitignoring, and an SDK pinned at 0.2.136 while `main` already expected 0.2.152.

The structural lesson concerns what a sweep's *scope* implies. The closeout routine reported "clear to sign off" repeatedly while an unmerged branch sat in a repository the sweep did not visit, which means the verdict was locally truthful and globally wrong — the same shape as a backup reporting OK while the SSD it would have copied to was unmounted, or a manifest-driven job succeeding over a folder it never enumerated. A sweep's clean verdict carries exactly as much assurance as its enumeration is complete, and the fix here was to widen the enumeration to nested `~/.claude` repositories rather than to change any check. The five remaining parked repositories are the known residual, and naming them converts an invisible condition into a work queue.

The branch-drift condition has a timing remedy established elsewhere in this knowledge base: open the pull request the same day, because otherwise the next sync reports the project's state from `main` and understates it. The compiler's 17 days is the long-tail version of the 38-commit `step1-triage` stranding, and both show that the cost is not paid once at discovery but continuously, every time a tool reads the mainline tip.

- [[concepts/sync-commits-mask-most-recent-work]] — The adjacent failure: commit metadata misrepresenting where human attention actually went.

# Shutdown-Induced dlopen Failure Reads as a Broken Install

A memsearch index failure flagged at session start was traced to machine shutdown rather than to memsearch itself. The Mac restarted at 07:46:56; a session-end hook had started background indexing, and macOS refuses to `dlopen` libraries while the system is shutting down, so `onnxruntime` failed to load. The install was unchanged since 5 August. A test index over `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts` returned `Indexed 94 chunks` at exit 0, confirming health. The proposed one-line fix is to add "system is shutting down" to the transient-error list in `~/.claude/hooks/memsearch-sync.js`.

## Key Points

- **The error named the loader, not the defect.** `onnxruntime` failing to load looks identical to a broken or half-installed dependency; the actual cause was the operating system declining dynamic loads during shutdown.
- **The timing is the diagnostic.** Correlating the failure with the 07:46:56 restart, and noting the install was untouched since 5 August, settled the cause before any change was made.
- **The failure occurred before memsearch opened its database** — no partial writes and no stale lock file, so there was no cleanup to perform.
- **Hook output is truncated at 300 characters, hiding the real traceback.** Full output goes to `.memsearch-index.log`, but each run overwrites it, so the evidence must be captured before the next run or it is gone.
- **The fix belongs in the transient-error list, not in the indexer.** Adding "system is shutting down" to `~/.claude/hooks/memsearch-sync.js` suppresses a false alarm at the layer that classifies errors; because Codex shares the file via symlink, one edit covers both harnesses.

## Details

This is a clean instance of an error naming the transport rather than the cause. A `dlopen` failure is the loader reporting that it could not bring a library into the process, which is a true statement that says nothing about whether the library is present, correct, or compatible — and the first reading of such a message is almost always "the dependency is broken." Resisting that reading required establishing the environment's state at the moment of failure: the machine was mid-restart, and macOS declines dynamic loads in that window. Once that is known, the install's provenance (unchanged since 5 August) stops being merely reassuring and becomes evidence, because an install that has not moved cannot have newly broken. The same walk-the-dependency-chain-first discipline resolved a memsearch timeout that was a stopped Docker Milvus container, and a regex error that was really a `None` from a mis-decoded subprocess.

The classification question is what makes the fix durable rather than cosmetic. A shutdown-time indexing failure is not a defect to repair; it is an expected consequence of running background work during a window when the OS withdraws a capability. The right response is therefore to teach the error classifier that this message is transient, which stops the false alarm at session start without suppressing genuine load failures that carry different text. The alternative explicitly considered — change nothing and accept repeat false alarms — is defensible but pays a recurring cost in attention each time the banner appears and has to be re-diagnosed. The symlink detail matters because it determines the blast radius of the one-line edit: Codex shares `memsearch-sync.js`, so the fix propagates without a second change.

The instrumentation gotcha is the most portable finding. A hook that truncates its error at 300 characters is reporting a prefix of the evidence, and the prefix is typically the generic wrapper message rather than the traceback that identifies the cause. Worse, the full log is single-slot: `.memsearch-index.log` is overwritten on every run, so the window for recovering the real error closes at the next invocation. Any debugging of a hook failure must therefore begin by securing the log copy, because the ordinary reflex — re-run it and watch — destroys the artifact being sought.

- [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]] — The accumulated catalogue of memsearch failure causes, nearly all uninformative from the error text alone.
- [[concepts/memsearch-indexing-lock-docker-dependency]] — The dependency-chain-first rule that applies directly here.

# Windows Scheduled Task Re-Registration as the Fallback Fix

A Windows scheduled task `\Eric\Refresh All Data` was created to run `_INBOX\refresh_all_data.bat` daily, then needed its trigger moved from 6:00 AM to 10:00 AM. The one-line `Set-ScheduledTask` route failed with "The system cannot find the file specified," and the recorded fallback is to re-register the task with `Register-ScheduledTask ... -Force` — which replaces the user's own task and therefore needs no administrator rights. A four-step diagnostic was supplied because the error message is ambiguous between two different missing files.

## Key Points

- **The normal retime is one non-admin line:** `Set-ScheduledTask -TaskPath "\Eric\" -TaskName "Refresh All Data" -Trigger (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At 10am)`, verified with `Get-ScheduledTaskInfo ... | Select-Object NextRunTime`.
- **`Register-ScheduledTask ... -Force` is the fallback** when `Set-ScheduledTask` is denied or cannot find the task; because `-Force` replaces a task the user owns, elevation is not required.
- **"File cannot be found" is ambiguous** — it can mean the task path or name is wrong, *or* that the `.bat` target path is missing. Both must be checked, which is why the diagnostic is four steps: list tasks matching `*Refresh*`, `Test-Path` the bat, re-register with `-Force`, then read `NextRunTime`.
- **A `.bat` launched by Task Scheduler closes its window on exit**, so its output is invisible; run the bat by hand to see whether the ForcePlate and Perch steps print `OK`.
- **The old failing `Refresh_All_Data` task was left in place** rather than removed, because deletion needs admin rights and the task does no harm — removal was recorded as a separate action item.
- **The STATUS file was written to say the 10:00 AM change was unconfirmed** rather than asserting the new time, keeping the record honest about what had actually been verified.

## Details

The ambiguity of the error message is the finding worth carrying forward. A scheduled-task cmdlet reporting that a file cannot be found is describing a failed lookup without saying which lookup failed — the task identity it was asked to modify, or the executable the task points at. Those two causes have entirely different fixes (correct the path/name versus repair or restore the target script), and guessing wrong wastes a round trip on a machine that is often being operated remotely through a handoff note. Enumerating both candidates up front, with a concrete command for each, is what makes the diagnostic usable by someone who is not currently looking at the failure. This is the same shape as a `dlopen` error naming the loader rather than the cause: the message is true about the layer that stopped and silent about why.

The invisible-output problem compounds it. Because Task Scheduler closes the `.bat` window on exit, the scheduled path produces no observable evidence of what the inner ForcePlate and Perch steps did, which means a task that registers correctly and runs on time can still be failing silently inside. The remedy adopted — run the bat by hand and look for `OK` from each step — splits the question into "does the task fire?" (answerable from `NextRunTime` and task state) and "does the work succeed?" (answerable only from the script's own output). That split mirrors the broader rule that a scheduler's status field answers a narrower question than operational health, and that the durable log, not the task state, is the contract.

Two restraint decisions round the session out. The old failing task was left alone because removing it requires elevation it cannot be given, and because an inert duplicate costs nothing except the reporting confusion of appearing in a task list — the same residual-reporting hazard as a still-registered no-op job after a cutover. And the STATUS file was written to record the 10:00 AM retime as *unconfirmed* rather than done, because the diagnostic's outcome had not been reported back. Asserting the new time would have made a future reader treat an open question as settled.

- [[concepts/windows-backup-task-trigger-gotchas]] — The accumulated Task Scheduler gotchas, including `schtasks /Change` being unable to add a schedule and triggerless tasks reading `Ready` forever.
- [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]] — Why absolute executable paths are required in the minimal spawn environment.

# Retry the Page, Not the Run: Perch Pull Timeout Fix

The `perch-pull` job was failing intermittently because a 30-second per-page timeout combined with a whole-pull restart turned any single slow response into a total run failure. Between 26 September and 1 October this produced 20 timeout events and three complete run failures (9/26, 9/27, 10/1). The fix was to retry each slow page individually rather than restarting the pull, justified by the observation that timeouts struck random pages — including first requests — which indicates an intermittently slow server rather than a specific bad page.

## Key Points

- **The evidence selected the fix.** Timeouts landing on random pages, including first requests, rules out a particular malformed page and points at server-side slowness; a per-page retry is the response that matches that cause.
- **Whole-pull restart was the amplifier, not the timeout.** A 30-second limit on one page escalating to a failed run is what converted 20 transient events into three outright failures.
- **No data was ever lost.** Later runs caught up, so the failures cost latency and alert noise rather than records — which is what made a measured fix affordable instead of urgent.
- **Retries cannot fix authentication.** A bad login token still fails immediately, so the retry path must not be allowed to mask or churn on an auth error.
- **A sibling session was already working the problem.** Its work was read first rather than repeated, after a check for another session on the same issue.

## Details

The diagnostic move here is to read the *distribution* of failures rather than any single failure. Twenty timeouts scattered across random page positions, with first requests among them, is a different signature from twenty timeouts on page 47; the first says the dependency is sometimes slow, the second says one request is malformed or oversized. Only the first signature licenses a blanket per-page retry, because retrying a genuinely bad page just re-fails more expensively. Establishing this before changing the code is the same discipline as correlating a `dlopen` failure with a machine restart, or checking a job's newest run before rerunning it — the cheap observation that determines whether the obvious fix is the right one.

The structural defect was the escalation path. A per-page timeout is a reasonable guard; restarting the entire pull when one page exceeds it is what makes the guard destructive, because it discards all completed work and re-exposes every page to the same intermittent risk, so the probability of a clean run falls as the pull gets longer. Narrowing the retry to the failing unit keeps the guard's protective value while removing its amplification — the same reasoning as resolving a blocked action at the narrowest sufficient rung rather than with a blanket bypass. The explicit note that authentication failures still fail immediately is the necessary boundary on that narrowing: a retry loop that cannot distinguish "slow" from "rejected" will hammer a dead credential and report the wrong class of problem.

That no data was lost is worth stating as part of the record rather than as an aside. It establishes the failure's true cost — alert noise and delayed freshness, not missing rows — which is what justified spending the session on a correct per-page fix instead of a fast workaround. It also means the three "full run failures" were, in operational terms, deferred successes, and a monitor reporting them as hard failures was overstating the severity.

# Session-End Hooks Run Inside the Shutdown Window

Work started by a session-end hook, or left running in the background when a session ends, executes in a window where the host is withdrawing capabilities and the session's own lifetime is expiring. Two independent 2026-10-08 observations make the point: a session-end hook kicked off background memsearch indexing during a machine restart, and macOS refused to `dlopen` `onnxruntime`, producing a session-start error for a healthy install; and a background "landed files" ledger scan was killed by a session restart (exit code -1) mid-closeout. The durable rule is that any deliverable depending on background work must be written to a durable file before the session can end.

## Key Points

- **The shutdown window is hostile to newly started work.** macOS declines dynamic library loads during shutdown, so a hook-launched indexer fails on load through no fault of its own.
- **Background scans do not survive a session restart.** The ledger scan exited -1 with nothing recoverable from the process itself.
- **Nothing was lost in the ledger case only because the output already existed elsewhere** — the changed-file list lived in the handoff document, so the scan's death cost time rather than information.
- **The remedy is ordering, not retry:** write the durable artifact first, then let the background job refine or confirm it, so a reaped job degrades the result instead of erasing it.
- **These failures are resource and lifetime events, not defects**, and should be classified as such before anyone debugs the code that happened to be running.

## Details

Both failures share a cause that is invisible in the error text: the process was running at a moment when its environment was being dismantled. A `dlopen` refusal and an exit code of -1 are each accurate reports from the layer that stopped, and neither says "the machine was shutting down" or "the session that owned me ended." That is why the first reading of both is a code defect, and why the correct first move is to establish what the host was doing at the timestamp — the same discipline that identified a reaped background job as memory pressure rather than a crash, and a stalled Drive-reading script as a sleep freeze rather than a hang.

The ordering remedy deserves to be stated positively. A closeout deliverable that is *produced* by a background scan is hostage to the session surviving long enough; a closeout deliverable that is *written first* and then checked by a background scan survives the scan's death with its content intact. The 2026-10-08 ledger case accidentally had the good property — the changed-file list was already in the handoff document — and that accident is what turned a killed job into a non-event. Generalising it means treating "the background job is the source of this artifact" as a design smell during any session-end sequence, and preferring hours-scale or crash-prone work to be re-sited into a scheduled job with its own durable log rather than run inside a session at all.

The hook-launched-indexer case adds a second, narrower prescription: when a hook is known to start work in the shutdown window, its error classifier should treat shutdown-specific messages as transient rather than surfacing them as failures at the next session start. Otherwise every restart manufactures an alarm that has to be re-diagnosed, and the operator learns to discount a channel that will eventually carry a real failure.

# Same File, Both Machines: Keep Both Sides

When both the Mac and the Windows laptop write the same shared file on the same day, the correct resolution depends on what the file *is*, and the distinction that recurs most often is content versus metadata. On 2026-10-08 a `daily-backup` failure was traced to exactly this condition — both machines had written to `~/.claude/global-memory` on 10/7, and git refused to overwrite the unsaved Mac changes. Two conflicts were resolved in opposite ways within the same merge: `transcripts/2026-10-07.md` kept both machines' notes, while `transcripts/.memsearch-last-run` kept only the newest timestamp and discarded the older Windows entry.

## Key Points

- **Content files keep both sides.** A daily log or transcript accumulates independent observations, so each machine's lines are information the other does not have; discarding either loses facts.
- **Metadata files take the newest value.** `.memsearch-last-run` records a single current state, so union-merging it is meaningless and newest-wins is the only sensible rule.
- **The conflict surfaces as a backup failure, not a merge prompt.** `daily-backup` reported the repo as behind/blocked because git would not overwrite uncommitted Mac changes — the merge was the prerequisite, not the symptom.
- **Tier A memory files are auto-injected per machine**, which is what makes simultaneous writes routine rather than exceptional, so this friction is structural and recurring.
- **The resolution needs a human decision on the metadata case.** Git merge plus a durable save handles the mechanics, but which timestamp or flag wins is a judgment the tooling cannot make.
- **Validation was deliberately deferred** to the next scheduled run rather than forced with a manual backup, on the grounds that the scheduled run is the real test.

## Details

The content-versus-metadata split is the operational form of a broader rule: the artifact's kind, not a blanket policy, selects the merge verb. Across the cross-machine conflicts recorded in this knowledge base the correct verbs have included discard (CRLF-only differences), union (append-only transcripts), merge-by-key (accumulating data tables), and deduplicate (router index lines) — and a single global "newest wins" or "Mac wins" rule would have silently destroyed data in at least two of those cases. The 2026-10-08 session is a compact demonstration because both verbs were needed inside one merge: keeping both sides of the daily log preserved two machines' independent session notes, while keeping both sides of a last-run timestamp would have produced a file with two mutually exclusive claims about the same state.

The failure's presentation is worth separating from its cause. The visible symptom was a `daily-backup` error, which routes attention toward the backup system; the actual condition was an unmerged shared repository with uncommitted local changes, which git correctly declined to clobber. A backup job that cannot push a repo it is responsible for is reporting truthfully about its own stage while saying nothing about the underlying two-writer conflict, and the same `repo-behind-blocked` shape has appeared repeatedly on `global-memory`. Reading the error as "backup broken" rather than "repo needs a merge" sends the fix to the wrong layer.

The deferred validation is a small but deliberate discipline. Having merged and saved, the session chose not to run a manual backup to prove the fix, reserving the next scheduled 10/9 run as the confirmation. That matches the established rule that fixes are not their own confirmation and that an error log should be cleared only after a verified clean run — and it leaves a named, checkable clearing condition rather than an assumption. Three unrelated errors were explicitly carried forward unfixed (memsearch-sync against Milvus from 10/6, a nightly-digest send failure from 10/6, and a gps-pull exit 4), keeping them visible rather than folding them into the same cleanup.

# Connection: The Shutdown Window Is a Cause, Not a Defect

## The Connection

Four failures across this stack were produced by the host withdrawing a capability rather than by any bug in the code that happened to be running: macOS refusing to `dlopen` `onnxruntime` because the machine was shutting down; a background ledger scan exiting -1 because the session that owned it restarted; a background job reaped under memory pressure; and a Drive-reading script frozen by Mac sleep and staying frozen after wake. In every case the reported error names the layer that stopped — a loader, an exit code, a missing progress line — and says nothing about the environmental state that stopped it.

## Key Insight

There is a diagnostic ordering that these four share and that the generic "walk the dependency chain" rule does not supply: **before reading any code, establish what the host was doing at the failure's timestamp.** Was it shutting down, sleeping, under memory pressure, or ending the session that owned the process? That question is cheap, is answerable from restart times and job timestamps, and when it comes back positive it terminates the investigation — because the correct response is not a fix at all.

The second half of the insight is that the right response splits by direction. Where the failure is a *false alarm* about healthy work — the `dlopen` refusal on an install untouched since 5 August — the remedy belongs in the error classifier, teaching it that this message is transient so the alarm stops recurring at every restart. Where the failure *lost work* — the killed ledger scan — the remedy is ordering: write the durable artifact first so a reaped job degrades the result rather than erasing it, or re-site the work into a scheduled job that owns its own lifetime and log. Neither remedy touches the code that produced the error message, which is exactly why reading that code first is the expensive mistake.

What makes this worth stating separately from [[connections/an-error-names-the-transport-not-the-cause]] is that a dependency-chain walk assumes the dependency is a *thing* — Docker, Milvus, a network, a file. Here the missing dependency is a *moment*: the capability existed before and after, and was unavailable only during a window. Nothing in the chain is broken, so a chain walk comes back clean and the investigator concludes the error must be real.

## Evidence

- 2026-10-08: the Mac restarted at 07:46:56 while a session-end hook was running background indexing; macOS refused the dynamic load and `onnxruntime` failed. The install was unchanged since 5 August, and a test index returned `Indexed 94 chunks` at exit 0. The proposed fix adds "system is shutting down" to the transient-error list — classifier, not indexer.
- 2026-10-08: a background "landed files" ledger scan was killed by a session restart (exit -1) mid-closeout; nothing was lost only because the changed-file list already lived in the handoff document. The recorded rule: write closeout deliverables to a durable file first.
- 2026-09-24: Claude Code reaped a background job under host memory pressure; the notification was explicitly classified as a resource event, with restarting discouraged.
- 2026-10-06: `landed.py` showed no progress because Mac sleep froze it three minutes in and the freeze survived wake; `caffeinate` plus a re-run finished in about four minutes.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
